# Continuous integration and repository hygiene

The contract auditor chapter showed one check — `test_scripts()` — turning a documented rule into a build gate. This chapter widens the view to everything a consumer repository should check on every push: that no data slipped into git, that no secret did either, that the provenance sidecars it commits are well-formed, that the analysis code honours the contract, that the vendored toolkit is the vintage the repo claims, and that the project's own functions still do what their tests say. It also sets out how the repository's `.gitignore` keeps data out in the first place, because continuous integration (CI) can only catch what the ignore rules let through.

Everything here ships as copyable material in the toolkit repository, so a new project adopts it by copying files rather than by reading this chapter twice:

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| `.gitignore` rules, with the reasoning and the checks | [`docs/gitignore_guidelines.md`](https://github.com/unicef-drp/cso-toolkit/blob/develop/docs/gitignore_guidelines.md) |
| `.gitignore` templates | `templates/gitignore/research-project.gitignore`, `templates/gitignore/official-stats.gitignore` |
| CI principles and the full menu | [`docs/ci_cd_guidelines.md`](https://github.com/unicef-drp/cso-toolkit/blob/develop/docs/ci_cd_guidelines.md) |
| GitHub Actions workflows | `templates/workflows/ci-hygiene.yml`, `ci-contract-audit.yml`, `ci-r-tests.yml`, `ci-manuscript.yml` |
| testthat skeleton for a non-package project | `templates/testthat/` |

## Data stay out; their provenance goes in

The rule the rest of the chapter enforces fits in one line: **data never enter git, and the provenance sidecars that say exactly which bytes each result came from always do.** Data live in the deposit — the Teams folder and its Z: mirror, the microdata archive, Gitea LFS — and `dw_fetch_inputs()` fills a local, gitignored inputs folder from it, checking each copy's SHA-256 (see the IO chapter). What git holds is the record. Every `dw_save()` output carries a `<file>.provenance.json` sidecar with the file's hash, schema, writer and mode, and through `metadata.inputs` the hashes of the inputs it was built from ([Appendix B](../appendices/b-provenance-schema.qmd)). Committing the sidecars puts that record under version control while the data stay out, so a reviewer can tell from git alone which bytes produced a result, and `dw_provenance_diff()` can tell whether a re-run reproduced it.

A sidecar sits next to its file when the file is inside the repository but ignored (`data/derived/panel.csv.provenance.json` is tracked; `panel.csv` is not). Microdata kept outside the repository get their sidecars under `data/provenance/<path>/`, mirroring where the file lives, so a sidecar for `S:\datalib-edu\KEN\2022\hh.dta` is committed as `data/provenance/S/datalib-edu/KEN/2022/hh.dta.provenance.json`.

The `.gitignore` pattern that implements this has four kinds of line, and the second is the one people drop:

```gitignore
data/**                       # ignore everything below data/
!data/**/                     # re-include the directories
!data/**/README.md            # then only these files
!data/**/.gitkeep
!data/**/*.provenance.json
!data/**/input_manifest.*
```

Git cannot re-include a file whose parent directory is excluded: to save time it never looks inside an excluded directory, so a `!` rule for a file in one is never consulted. Because `data/**` also matches the sub-directories, `!data/**/` (the trailing slash means "directories only") is what lets git look inside them again; the files there stay ignored unless a later `!` line names them. For the same reason the folder rule is `data/**`, never `data/` — the latter excludes the directory itself and nothing below it can come back. The templates repeat the block for `inputs/`, `_apis/` (the API cache) and `_frozen/` (frozen URL downloads), then ignore data formats wherever they appear (`*.dta`, `*.rds`, `*.parquet`, …), secrets and personal configuration (`.env`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `user_config.yml`, `.Renviron`), and the build noise of R, Python, Stata, Quarto and LaTeX.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check the rules, not your memory of them
`git check-ignore -v <path>` prints the line that decides a path. `git ls-files -i -c --exclude-standard` lists tracked files the rules now say should be ignored — after adopting a template it must print nothing. `git rm --cached -- <path>` untracks a file without deleting it. History still holds anything committed before; removing it from history is a separate decision, taken with the repository owner (and the data owner, for confidential microdata), and a leaked secret is rotated first, whatever happens to history.
:::

The ignore file is the safety net, not the first line of defence. That is the staging habit: never `git add -A` or `git add .`; stage by path (`git add -- R/clean.R results/t1.csv results/t1.csv.provenance.json`) and read `git diff --cached --stat` before committing. CI is the backstop that catches what both miss.

## Design principles

Ten principles shape the menu. Each earns its place by a failure it prevents.

1. **CI never needs real data.** Tests use tiny synthetic fixtures. Reproduction against real data runs locally in reviewer mode, and its evidence — the `dw_provenance_diff()` status, `dw_check_deposit()` output, a `dw_compare()` summary — goes in the pull request. Data must not be on a hosted runner, and a check that needs data cannot run on every push.
2. **Default checks are fast, under ten minutes.** A check people wait for gets skipped.
3. **The same checks run locally with one command.** A failure reproducible on your machine gets fixed before the push.
4. **Required checks gate the protected branches.** A check that can be merged around is advice, not a gate.
5. **Every bug fix ships a regression test** that fails on the old code and names the issue. The bug cannot return silently, and the test records what went wrong.
6. **Least privilege, pinned actions.** Workflows start from `permissions: contents: read`; actions are pinned to a version. A compromised dependency should not be able to write to the repository or alter results unnoticed.
7. **No secrets in logs.** Prefer checks that need no secret; scanners redact. Logs are readable by everyone with access to the repository.
8. **Fail with an actionable message**, in the toolkit's WHAT / Why / Fix envelope (see the provenance and errors chapter). A red check that says how to turn it green costs minutes.
9. **Spend minutes where they buy something.** Default to `ubuntu-latest`; run Windows and macOS on a schedule or on release. Private repositories pay for minutes, and Windows minutes count double and macOS minutes ten times.
10. **CI is documentation.** A badge and a short README section listing what runs and how to run it locally.

## The default menu

The checks come in three tiers. Tier 0 goes in every repository; Tier 1 in every repository with code; Tier 2 when it earns its keep.

| Tier | Check | Template | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | No data or secrets tracked outside the allowlist | `ci-hygiene.yml` | required |
| 0 | No tracked file over 50 MB | `ci-hygiene.yml` | required |
| 0 | Secret scan of the full history (gitleaks, redacted) | `ci-hygiene.yml` | required |
| 0 | Provenance sidecars parse and carry the core keys | `ci-hygiene.yml` | required |
| 0 | Contract audit, `test_scripts(error_on_violation = TRUE)` | `ci-contract-audit.yml` | required |
| 0 | Toolkit vintage: manifest well-formed, `cso_toolkit_check()` offline | `ci-contract-audit.yml` | required |
| 1 | R tests (testthat; R CMD check for a package) | `ci-r-tests.yml` | required |
| 1 | lintr | `ci-r-tests.yml` | advisory |
| 2 | Manuscript build and page limit | `ci-manuscript.yml` | advisory |
| 2 | Site deploy, `renv` status, cross-language conformance, scheduled drift checks | see `docs/ci_cd_guidelines.md` | advisory |

Three of the Tier 0 checks lean on earlier chapters. The **sidecar check** validates the shape [Appendix B](../appendices/b-provenance-schema.qmd) documents: `path`, `format`, `written_at`, `dw_mode`, and a 64-character hex `sha256` for an R or Python sidecar; `datasignature` in place of the hash for a Stata one; `url`, `fetched_at`, `dw_mode` and `sha256` for an API-fetch sidecar. It does not re-compute hashes: the data are not in the repository, so the bytes are checked locally or in reviewer mode, where `dw_read_provenance()`, `dw_check_deposit()` and `dw_provenance_diff()` have the files to hash. The **contract audit** is the job [the contract auditor chapter](43-contract-auditor-ci.qmd) sketched, with one change: it sources the helpers *vendored* in `00_functions/` instead of installing the toolkit from GitHub, so CI audits with exactly the vintage the repository runs ([the vendoring model](41-vendoring.qmd)). The **vintage check** reads `.toolkit_manifest.yml`, confirms every `vendored:` file is present, and runs `cso_toolkit_check()` in reviewer mode, failing when `pulled_version` is behind `target_version`. A newer upstream tag is not a failure — refreshing remains the producer's decision ([versioning and releases](44-versioning-release.qmd)).

## testthat in every R repository

A sector pipeline or a paper is not an R package, so it has no `R CMD check` to run its tests. The `templates/testthat/` skeleton fills that gap with a runner, `tests/testthat.R`, that works without a `DESCRIPTION`: it puts the session in reviewer mode (so a test that reaches for the network or a canonical deposit fails instead of fetching), sources the vendored helpers and the project's function files, and calls `testthat::test_dir()`, exiting non-zero on any failure. The same command runs locally and in CI.

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```r
# Locally, from the repository root (CI runs the same):
#   Rscript tests/testthat.R

# A regression test names the issue and fails on the pre-fix code.
test_that("regression #12: codes with stray whitespace or lower case are kept", {
  ind <- read_fixture("indicators_synthetic.csv")   # tiny, synthetic
  out <- merge_country_names(ind, countries)
  expect_setequal(out$TIME_PERIOD[out$country == "Kenya"], c(2021, 2022))
})

test_that("an unknown code fails with a WHAT / Why / Fix error", {
  err <- expect_error(merge_country_names(bad, countries))
  expect_envelope(err, "merge_country_names")
})
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```python
# No Python skeleton ships yet. Use pytest with the same rules:
# synthetic fixtures under tests/fixtures/, a regression test per fixed
# bug named after the issue, errors asserted on the
# "[<scope>.<function>] ... Fix:" envelope, and the session configured
# with dw_mode="reviewer", dw_apis_allowed=False.
```

#### Stata {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```stata
* No Stata test runner ships. Stata code is covered by the conformance
* harness where it applies and by review; the hygiene and sidecar checks
* still run, since they read only files.
```

:::

The example in the skeleton is the pattern to copy rather than the function to keep: a small project function, a fixture that carries the very codes that once broke it, and a test whose title names the issue. Run against the old implementation — an inner join on raw codes — that test fails; against the fix it passes. The skeleton follows the toolkit's own suite: helpers in `helper-*.R`, session state set through a local setter that restores on exit, errors asserted with `expect_envelope()`.

## Required checks and the gitflow

Tier 0 and Tier 1 jobs are marked as required status checks on both `develop` and `main`, so neither a feature pull request nor a release pull request can merge red (see `docs/git_workflow.md` for the gitflow itself). Advisory checks — lintr, the manuscript build, scheduled jobs — report on the pull request but never block it. Two operational details matter. GitHub matches a required check by its job name, so the templates give each job a stable `name:`. And a required workflow must not carry a `paths:` filter: when a pull request touches no matching path the workflow never runs, and its required check waits forever. Path filters belong on advisory workflows only, which is why the manuscript template is advisory.

---

The contract auditor made one rule enforceable; this chapter makes the rest of the repository's floor enforceable in the same way. The `.gitignore` keeps data out, the committed sidecars keep their provenance in, and a handful of fast checks — none of which needs data, credentials or network — turn both, and the contract, into gates a pull request has to pass.
